request: Let agents upload a CSV to bulk-create tickets.

labels.why: A CSV contains several creates, so a bad row needs a defined effect on the other rows.
The agent needs a response that identifies a failed CSV record and its validation error so the record can be corrected.
Single creates allocate fresh IDs even for identical inputs, so the import must define what repeated values do both within the file and against existing tickets.
Every caller of single create can supply only title, requester and an allowed priority, so applying those same checks to each row preserves the caller's authority.

labels.applies_part: Define which callers may upload and the trusted access boundary on which that decision relies.
labels.why: The request names agents, but enforcing an independent import privilege would add a distinction the service lacks, since X-Actor only attributes changes.
The header maps cells to the required title and requester and optional priority, so missing or unexpected columns need defined errors.
Encoding, record separators and quoting determine which values reach the single-ticket validator and which record an error identifies.
Each create appends an audit entry and queues a real requester notification, so the failure policy must account for earlier effects, including irreversible deliveries.
The service already enforces MAX_BODY_BYTES, and the upload must bound the work it accepts and specify the response when that bound is exceeded.
Zero bytes, a valid header with no records and a single record are distinct inputs with observable ticket counts and responses.
Replaying rows through ordinary create allocates new IDs and queues fresh notifications, so agents need to know the consequence of resubmission.
The worker delivers outbox events, while background CSV execution and a later completion signal would add an import job workflow beyond a bounded upload.
Each created ticket queues a requester notification and the worker attempts every due event per tick, so the import must account for the resulting delivery burst.

labels.applies_part: Specify that imported tickets start open, default to normal priority and receive server-generated creation and update timestamps as in single create.
labels.why: Status, priority and timestamps already exist, while defaulting an assignee would introduce ticket assignment.

labels.applies_part: Define where the raw CSV and any temporary copies reside during processing and when they are discarded, including on failure.
labels.why: Requester data enters through the upload, while downloading the original later would require retaining and serving a new artifact.
Title and requester are text and priority uses fixed literals, so date-like or numeric-looking cells need a literal interpretation independent of locale.
Every accepted creation belongs in the existing per-ticket history with its request actor, field values and creation time.
Cancelling active imports and selectively replaying failures are additional controls that a bounded upload with row-level results can omit.

labels.applies_part: Set and verify a processing-time bound for a maximum-size accepted CSV under stated runtime and data-file conditions.
labels.why: Saving the whole store on each create affects request duration, while live progress would require an additional way to observe an import in flight.
Bulk creation extends the single-create API contract and must preserve that path and the contents of all pre-existing tickets.
Imported text must respect existing field limits, and formula-like titles can already reach spreadsheet-readable output through the tab-separated operator listing.
